reverse_outline.summary: A shopper's confirmed order at a fictional outdoor brand is the moment several merchant systems must start working to deliver the right parcel on time.
The confirmation bundles several promises that depend on other systems' answers, so a checkout can succeed while committing the merchant to something it cannot keep.
A Black Friday oversell at the same shop shows the failure happening in the handoffs between systems, while each system itself stayed up.
What the book does (follows the order end to end and explains who owns each fact, how changes spread and how disagreements are handled as the merchant grows) and the two ways to read it.
The intended readers: newcomers to commerce architecture, in four kinds of role (merchant staff, software vendor, agency or consultancy, leadership).
The prior knowledge assumed: general software basics, no commerce experience.
Terms and mechanisms are explained in the chapters that need them, and gathered in a glossary.
The author's speaking position: an architect advising growing merchants, who flags personal judgement in the first person with reasons and conditions.
The book redefines a commerce platform as the whole set of systems that make and keep promises to a customer, not a single product, and lists those systems.
Promises are made in one system and kept in others, with a fallible handoff in between.
The central claim that most commerce failures are promises one system made and another could not keep, shown by three incidents at the fictional merchant.
Architecture is defined as answering three questions for every promise (lead-in to a table).
A name-only index of sixteen recurring failure patterns in four families (truth, integration, platform and change, governance), detailed on the next page.
The patterns occur in chains that start at the joins, the merchant's incidents are mapped onto named patterns, and chapters name the patterns they address.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Four Scale Stages, and Why Every Chapter Compares Them ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The same three questions have different right answers at different business sizes, so the book compares decisions across four scale stages.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Four Scale Stages, and Why Every Chapter Compares Them ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A business's shape, not its revenue, determines its stage; the revenue bands are only illustrative.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Four Scale Stages, and Why Every Chapter Compares Them ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Every main-body chapter has a per-stage comparison section; and the commonest architectural mistake is a design suited to a different stage, as the merchant's troubles show.
The fictional merchant's profile: origin, 2026 revenue by channel, and the channel footprint that places it at the Omnichannel stage.
Its fragmented system landscape, with orders and product content each held in several places, and what the recurring incidents cost.
A new Head of Engineering, the reader's stand-in, arrives; and she launches the Waypoint program, which settles ownership first and then buys the missing central systems, in eight numbered decisions.
The merchant is a composite, not a disguised real company, and readers should translate its decisions to their own business.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Order's Journey as the Spine ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The book is organized around one order's journey, the shopper's jacket order, whose dates and facts stay fixed throughout.
The book's components (preface pages, eleven parts, appendix, reference pages), with each part asking one question (lead-in to a table).
Parts II to V follow the order in sequence and Part VI covers the links between systems; each chapter has a paragraph locating it in the order's journey.
Part I should not be skipped because it sets up the vocabulary and reference tables the later chapters rely on.
The fixed shape of every chapter in Parts II to VIII: five recurring questions, an opening scene, and closing take-aways, review questions and sources.
Part IX's four end-to-end journeys each run a fixed story through the architecture before and after the change program.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Start With the Decision in Front of You ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: How a reader with a pressing decision uses the routing table to find a starting chapter instead of reading in order.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Start With the Decision in Front of You ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Why the overselling row points to inventory: the fix is deciding who owns stock, not speeding up copies.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Start With the Decision in Front of You ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The toolkit gathers sixteen working templates; start with the one relevant to the current decision.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Book Leaves to Others ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Three neighbouring subjects (payment and ledger internals, operating a marketplace, AI agent internals) are covered only at the merchant's edge and left to companion books.
Chapters keep six kinds of statement apart so the reader can tell how much weight each sentence carries (lead-in to a table).
Two easily lost distinctions: the fictional merchant's figures are illustrations, not benchmarks, and fact-sounding recommendations remain recommendations.
Claims are dated because undated ones go stale, shown by a company's design reversal and by vendor interfaces changing on published dates.
Laws also take effect on dates, so the book dates every company and regulatory claim, flags old evidence and separates announced features from available ones.
Each chapter's closing take-aways are split into three tiers that show how much weight each conclusion carries (lead-in to a table).
The book's only three kinds of source material: dated public sources, verified research briefs, and the author's domain models used as maps rather than as facts about any company.
The book is vendor-neutral: the fictional merchant's systems are named by role, and real companies appear only as dated, sourced cases, not as answers.
No confidential or inside material is used; the fictional merchant fills gaps in the public record.
The book is a continually revised work in progress with a stated research cut-off date, and its 2027 story uses only dates published by then.
Each chapter links to the spec it was written against, open questions included, so the book should be read as current thinking with stated limits.
How the book was made with AI tools under the author's direction and review, where its sources live, and that the author takes responsibility for it.
Next steps for the two kinds of reader: the next pages in order, or the routing table for a waiting decision.
Closing: keep the order's five promises in mind, since all the book's devices ask which system makes a promise, which keeps it and how far that holds for your business, before any product choice.
